title: Kitchen Science Lab
goal: Your kid turns the kitchen into a real chemistry lab and solves a mystery: five white powders that look almost the same. They make a colour-changing juice from red cabbage, run fair tests with water and vinegar, build a results table, then identify a secret powder you hand them. No guessing allowed. Every test has to rule something out.
need: Five white powders: baking soda, baking powder, cornstarch, sugar and salt
Half a red cabbage, hot water and a strainer
Vinegar, lemon juice and warm water
Small clear cups or jars, teaspoons and masking tape for labels
A tray to catch spills, and paper for a results table

academics.subject: Reasoning
academics.text: ruling out until one answer fits

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: No hints about the secret powder, even when they're one test away and pleading. You handle the hot water and the stove, and the tray goes under everything. The fun is in figuring it out.

plan.what: Set up the lab and make the cabbage juice (Steps 1 and 2).
Run every test on the five suspects (Step 3).
Solve the mystery powder and test their own question (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.q: Two powders gave the same result
troubleshoot.a: That's the point. A test only rules things out. Look at the table and find a test where those two behave differently.

troubleshoot.q: They want to taste it to check
troubleshoot.a: Hold the lab rule: no tasting, ever. Real scientists don't taste unknown powders, and the tests can tell them everything.

troubleshoot.q: The cabbage juice came out blue
troubleshoot.a: Tap water can do that. Compare every cup with your plain-water cup and the test still works, or try bottled water.

lesson.text: Scientists don't guess. Every test rules something out, until only one answer fits.
lesson.before: It's white and powdery. It's probably sugar.

model.line: White and fine. That's true of all 5 suspects.
Only baking soda and baking powder fizz in vinegar. 3 suspects gone.
One more test, warm water, tells which. That's evidence, not a guess.

lesson.modelNote: The first try named a powder from how it looked, and all five look alike. The fix runs a test that rules three out, then one more to settle it.

steps.title: Set up the lab
steps.why: Good science starts with careful looking.
steps.kid: Your kid sets up a lab corner on a tray and labels five cups with the names of the suspects: baking soda, baking powder, cornstarch, sugar and salt. They put a spoonful in each, then look closely, rub a pinch between their fingers and write down what they notice about each one.
steps.you: Go over the lab rules together: no tasting, a tray under everything, a grown-up for anything hot.
ask: Which two look the most alike?
Could you tell them apart just by looking?
steps.tip: Rub cornstarch between your fingers: it squeaks and feels silky. Salt and sugar feel gritty. Clues are already appearing.

levels.explore: Describe each powder in a few words.
levels.develop: Write how each one looks and feels, and circle the ones that seem the same.
levels.extend: Use a magnifying glass and sketch the grains of each powder.

steps.title: Make the colour-changing juice
steps.why: Some liquids are acids, some are bases. Cabbage can tell.
steps.kid: Your kid chops the cabbage, you pour hot water over it, and after 15 to 30 minutes they strain out a purple juice. They add a splash to plain water first: that's the 'nothing happening' colour. Then they test lemon juice, vinegar and baking soda water, and line the cups up using the Cabbage colours card in the Lab Toolkit at the end of the guide.
steps.you: Handle the hot water. Then step back and let them name the colours.
ask: What colour did the lemon juice turn it?
steps.tip: Plain water is the 'control': what the juice looks like when nothing is changing it. Every other colour is compared to it.

levels.explore: Test 3 liquids and say which changed colour.
levels.develop: Test 5 liquids and sort them from acid to base.
levels.extend: Add baking soda water to pink vinegar juice a few drops at a time. When does it turn purple, and why?

steps.title: Run the tests
steps.why: A fair test is the same every time except the one thing you're testing.
steps.kid: Your kid draws a results table: the five suspects down the side, four tests across the top. For each powder they run the same four tests with the same amount, one level teaspoon: stir it into warm water, drop vinegar on it, add cabbage juice, and add about half a teaspoon of water to make a paste. They write what happens in every box.
steps.you: Help keep the amounts equal and the cups clean. Wipe the spoon between powders.
ask: Which powders did something in vinegar?
steps.tip: If the amount changes, the test isn't fair. Level the teaspoon with a knife every time.

levels.develop: Run all 4 tests and fill in the whole table.
levels.extend: Design a fifth test that tells sugar from salt without tasting or heat, like what's left when the water dries.

steps.title: Solve the mystery powder
steps.why: Now the table becomes a tool.
steps.kid: While your kid looks away, you put a spoonful of one suspect in a cup marked 'Mystery'. They use their results table and the Clue key card to choose each test until only one suspect is left, in as few tests as possible.
steps.you: Keep the secret. If it's down to sugar and salt, do the heat test yourself: a pinch of each in a dry pan on low. Sugar melts and browns, salt doesn't. Melted sugar burns badly, so no touching.
ask: What did that test rule out?
Why did you pick that test first?
steps.tip: Vinegar first splits the suspects into fizzers and non-fizzers. One test, two groups.

levels.develop: Solve three, and explain how you knew each time.
levels.extend: Solve a mystery that's a mix of two powders.

steps.title: Ask your own question
steps.why: Real scientists test questions nobody handed them.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a 'what would happen if' question from the Question ideas card or their own, like does warm vinegar fizz more than cold? They change just one thing, keep everything else the same using the Fair test card, predict, run it and share what they found with the family like a real scientist. Then they fill in Mystery solved at the end of the guide.
steps.you: Treat their question like real research. Ask what they're changing and what stays the same.
ask: What's the one thing you're changing?
steps.tip: If two things change and the result changes, you can't know which one did it. One change at a time.

levels.explore: Test one question and say what happened.
levels.develop: Predict first, test fairly and explain the result.
levels.extend: Test your change at 3 levels, like 1, 2 and 3 spoons. Does the result grow evenly?

conclusion.headline: They can tell five white powders apart.
conclusion.text: Tomorrow, put a spoonful of one powder in a cup and ask which it is. Watch which test they reach for first. If it's vinegar, they know one drop splits the five suspects into two groups, and they can tell you why.
conclusion.celebrate: Save your praise for the reveal: 'You didn't guess once. Every test crossed something off, and that's how you knew.'
extensions: Test a pantry mix, like pancake mix, and work out which suspects are inside
Use the cabbage juice to test every drink in the fridge
Write up a one-page lab report with a chart
Add a sixth suspect, like flour, and find a test that tells it apart

signs: They ask 'how do you know?' about everyday claims
They ask for a control before they trust a result
They notice small differences other people miss
makeItReal: If the bread doesn't rise or the cookies spread flat, ask what changed, and let them pick one thing to change on the next batch.
